title: Stellenbosch
description: South Africa's historic heart: mountain slopes, ocean breezes, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinotage.
L: Stellenbosch lies about 50 km east of Cape Town, in the Western Cape. It's surrounded by mountains, like the Simonsberg, Helderberg and Stellenbosch Mountain, with vineyards on slopes and valley floors. It has about 13,000 hectares of vines and around 150 wineries. Soils are mostly ancient granite and sandstone, among the oldest in the wine world.

Stellenbosch has a warm Mediterranean climate: dry summers, wet winters. False Bay, just to the south, sends cool sea breezes inland in the afternoon. The Cape Doctor, a strong south-easterly wind, cools vines and keeps them healthy. Mountain slopes add altitude and different exposures, so sites vary greatly.
False Bay breezes and the Cape Doctor
What cools Stellenbosch vineyards in the afternoon?
False Bay lies just south of the region.

Stellenbosch was founded in 1679 by Simon van der Stel, the Dutch governor of the Cape, making it South Africa's second oldest town. French Huguenots arrived in the 1680s with winemaking skills. Stellenbosch University, home of the country's main wine science department, created Pinotage in 1925. The Wine of Origin system began in 1973.

Cabernet Sauvignon is Stellenbosch's most important red, giving structured wines with blackcurrant, cedar, herbs and fresh acidity, often compared with Bordeaux. Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Shiraz and Pinotage also thrive. Bordeaux-style blends are a strength; estates like Kanonkop, Meerlust and Rustenberg are famous.

Chenin Blanc, called Steen locally, is widely planted, giving everything from fresh, fruity wines to rich, oaked old-vine wines. Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay thrive on cooler, higher sites. South Africa has more Chenin Blanc than any other country.

Look for wards on labels, like Simonsberg-Stellenbosch or Helderberg. They help you find specific sites within the region.

Stellenbosch Cabernet, especially from the slopes of the Simonsberg and Helderberg, combines ripe dark fruit with herbal, savoury notes and firm structure. Wards like Simonsberg-Stellenbosch and Jonkershoek Valley are known for it. Good examples age 15 to 20 years. Many call Stellenbosch South Africa's Cabernet capital.

Pinotage, a 1925 cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault, then called Hermitage, gives dark fruit, plum, mulberry and smoky notes. Kanonkop, in Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, is famous for it. A Cape blend is a red blend with a significant share of Pinotage, usually 30 to 70%, with Bordeaux grapes or Shiraz, giving South Africa its own blend style.

South Africa's Old Vine Project, started in 2016, certifies vineyards over 35 years old with a Certified Heritage Vineyards seal. Stellenbosch has old Chenin, Cinsault and Pinotage vines whose low yields give concentrated wines. The project has helped save many old vineyards from being replanted.

South Africa's Wine of Origin system, since 1973, has regions, districts and wards. Stellenbosch is a district; wards include Simonsberg-Stellenbosch, Jonkershoek Valley and Banghoek. A certification seal on the bottle guarantees origin, grape and vintage, each at least 85%. Estate wine must be grown and made on one property.

Stellenbosch Cabernet suits steak, lamb and game like springbok. Pinotage suits the braai, South African barbecue, especially boerewors sausage, and bobotie, a spiced Cape Malay mince dish. Chenin Blanc suits seafood, chicken and mild curries. Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees.
Which South African dish suits Pinotage?
Smoky grilled sausage suits Pinotage's fruit and smoke.
Bobotie, a spiced, baked minced meat dish with a custard topping, also suits off-dry Chenin Blanc.
